There is nothing wrong with civil discussion. It's quite elevating. What people are acting out against here is the perceived feeling of forced civil discussion. I unsubscribed from this verse a while back; but, as fate would have it, I somehow stumbled across it today. let me try to explain what my, I'm sure, well intentioned colleague /u/canopy probably meant to say below.

Voat, more or less, only exists today due to the mass migrations from reddit when the site started dictating how things should be said, when they could be said, and who could say these things. This rubbed a lot of people the wrong way. Historically, freedom of the individual has always been strongly valued in the US. After all, different views bring about different ideas and philosophies. It used to be that newspapers would print a relatively unbiased story and then people discussed the printed events and their opinions of it all. People who were raised in the lap of luxury would possibly have different views and articulate those views in a more sophisticated way than a sailor might, but neither aristocrat nor sailor would ever be shunned or banned from a pub for voicing their opinion in their respective common tongue. Enter the internet. Suddenly the world becomes very small and no longer are we living at a national level, we now live on a global level and opinions and philosophies become even more exponentially diverse. No longer are we at mere extremes of aristocrats and paupers, suddenly we can explore the philosophies of all manner of walks of life from every nook and cranny of the earth. Enter reddit. Suddenly there becomes an electronic version of a town pub. All these wonderful people from all walks of life find a place to congregate together and speak their minds. There were good times and there were bad times, but overall it was an astoundingly elevating experience. That is, until it became a place where speaking your mind became wrong if it didn't meet certain criteria. Then that criteria became increasingly more strict. Then simply talking in one area of the pub could lead to bans in other areas--or worse, be banned from the pub entirely...for talking. The pub suddenly became an unrecognizable place for those who sought to explore the inner minds of others. Some, not all, and sadly, not even most, people decided to leave in search of a new land where they could establish a new pub. A pub with an open door policy. A pub where both aristocrat and sailor could come back together to talk how each felt comfortable talking, in his own way. For surely an aristocrat could learn a thing or two from a sailor and likewise a sailor could also learn much from aristocrat. They may disagree, there may be struggle and strife, they may even have contempt for the others vernacular, but they still want to hear the other speak.

So when a sub like this starts suggesting that all the people in this corner of the pub start talking like aristocrats, the sailor's nervousness and knee-jerk reaction can not only be understood, but also sympathized with. Today, sir, you ask for everyone to speak in a certain manner, tomorrow you might ask people not to speak of certain things, and later you might even find a way to become exclusionary...and for what? How much more could you learn if you didn't tear out the offending pages of a math book? How much more could you contemplate if you could be mature enough to disregard foul talk as nothing more than the prose of the common folk? I certainly will not be a part of this corner of the pub for it breeds a more dangerous kind of insidiousness than can the other corner where, though it may be foul and vile, one still has free reign over their mind and tongue. Good day.
